```json
{
  "winner": "B",
  "reasons": [
    "The goal is one paying customer within 90 days. B fits that goal better. It is a self-serve $10-15/month personal purchase sold through cheap channels: a Product Hunt launch at $200-$2,000 and YouTube sponsorships at $20-$40 CPM. A depends on conference booths costing $3,000-$10,000 and on a per-practice sales cycle.",
    "A's own brief documents a nearly identical precedent, Cydoc, built by a clinically credentialed founder. It reached only four paying customers and $27,900 in 2024 revenue, mostly non-subscription. It needed $4,000-$6,000 in integration cost per practice and was estimated at 11 years to break even per practice. Its first sales call showed scope being renegotiated per practice. This is direct evidence that time-to-first-revenue is long in A's niche.",
    "A's regulatory overhead is heavier and recurs. It needs a HIPAA BAA for each customer, ongoing safeguards, and a legal review to stay out of FDA device scope. B needs only a one-time 1-2 hour privacy policy and ToS consult plus GDPR/CCPA export and delete mechanisms. A solo operator running agents can absorb B's setup much more easily.",
    "B's case against is real. The market is crowded with free or cheap incumbents (Obsidian, WorldBrain Memex), WorldBrain has not reached mainstream traction, and Tana pivoted. But these weigh on long-run scale more than on landing a first payer. The sourced Roam price of $15/month shows that individuals in this category are charged subscription prices.",
    "Both briefs show competitor pricing as their main willingness-to-pay signal. Neither has direct buyer-intent evidence. So the deciding factors are acquisition cost, sales-cycle length and regulatory drag, and A loses on all three."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "A's demand evidence is a single Reddit post from a PMHNP. The PMHNP is an employee, not a practice owner who would pay. The complaint is that the employer would not add more intake paperwork, not that anyone would pay for AI note software. A's Case For also claims competitors have 'apparent traction', but the brief gives no source for this. The only cited competitor facts are list prices, so actual traction counts as missing.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate. B's demand evidence is also thin: a 2020 HN comment and a researcher blog post, neither showing willingness to pay. B's market saturation means a first payer could still be hard to get. The pick rests mainly on A's documented Cydoc failure pattern and A's high-friction sales and regulatory path, not on strong positive evidence for B."
}
```
